submissions.scenario: Conditional sentences (Type 3) — the second-floor library at Target Yunusobod edition
submissions.text:
The second-floor library at Target Yunusobod is where I finally understood that conditionals are a way of arguing with the past. We had twenty minutes before the bell, and Ms. Rasulova asked us to rewrite the same regret twice: once as a third conditional and once as an excuse.

My first attempt was clean grammar and no honesty. "If I had started earlier, I would have finished the essay." True, but useless, because it stops at blame. My second attempt was longer: "If I had started earlier, I would have had time to interview my grandfather, and the essay would have had a real voice in it." Same grammar, different amount of thinking.

That is the test I now use. Does the sentence point at a decision I could repeat, or does it just point at me? Conditionals are not a time machine. They are a spotlight, and a spotlight can be aimed at a choice or at a person.

Why does this matter in a real exam? Because the examiner can tell the difference. A sentence that names a specific decision (leaving the house at 8:05, skipping the second draft, choosing the easier source) sounds like someone who was actually there. A sentence that says "I would have done better" sounds like a template.

I noticed the same pattern in the novel's regrets. The character who says "If I had spoken first" gets our sympathy, while the one who says "If things had been different" gets nothing, because he never names what he would have changed.

Next time I would write the third conditional first, then delete every word that only blames me, and see what survives. If nothing survives, the regret was never about a decision in the first place, was it?

submissions.scenario: Conditional sentences (Type 3) — a Yandex Go ride on Amir Temur Avenue edition
submissions.text:
I used to think the third conditional was just a longer way of saying sorry. In class we rewrote three regrets from the novel as third conditionals, starting with the sentence about the missed train, and that exercise changed how the grammar felt to me.

On the way home I took a Yandex Go ride along Amir Temur Avenue and the driver kept complaining about a passenger who cancelled. He said: "If I had waited two more minutes, I would have earned enough for the whole evening." He did not know he was producing a perfect third conditional while complaining, and I almost told him.

That moment made the rule click. The structure is "If + had + past participle, would have + past participle", but the useful part is what it selects: one decision out of a whole evening. His sentence did not describe the evening, it described the two minutes he kept replaying.

However, the grammar becomes dishonest if you use it to invent certainty about the past. Saying "if I had studied, I would have passed" pretends the result was guaranteed, when in reality the exam could have gone badly anyway. Conditionals give shape to regret, but they can also make a guess sound like a calculation.

My own regret is smaller and more concrete: I had 12 minutes before the metro at Yunusobod closed and I spent 10 of them looking for my card. If I had kept the card in my jacket, I would have caught the 21:40 train and would not have walked home.

For the rewrite I would cut the driver anecdote and keep the metro one, because the driver is a character while the metro is evidence.

submission.scenario: Persuasive paragraph structure — Chorsu Bazaar edition
submission.text:
Question first, answer second — that was the whole argument in Room 214 today. The paragraph that opened with a question kept my attention, while the other one lost me by line three.

In class we compared two paragraphs about the Chorsu Bazaar price negotiation, and Ms. Rasulova made us vote before revealing which one a person had written. I tried the same trick at my uncle's phone-repair stall near Chorsu. A customer walked in and asked for the cheapest screen I had. Instead of listing prices I asked: "Do you want the screen that lasts eight months or the one that lasts two?" He stopped, thought for about 30 seconds, and chose the longer-lasting one. Nobody in that conversation mentioned the word "quality", but that is exactly what we were negotiating.

However, the question-first approach fails when the customer already knows what they want. A man came in later asking for a specific battery model, and my question only annoyed him because it delayed the answer he had already decided on. So the technique is a tool for uncertainty, not a magic formula.

Why does this matter outside an exam? Because in a real bazaar nobody grades my paragraph. They either stay and listen or they walk to the next stall. The winning paragraph in class worked for the same reason it worked at the stall: it made the listener the subject of the sentence, not the product.

If my teacher disagreed, I would keep the Chorsu example but cut the second anecdote, because one precise story proves more than two vague ones.

submission.text:
In today's fast-paced world, effective communication plays a crucial role in both personal and professional success. Persuasive writing is a multifaceted skill that requires careful consideration of the audience, the purpose, and the structure of the argument.

Furthermore, it is important to note that a strong paragraph typically begins with a clear topic sentence. This sentence introduces the main idea and guides the reader through the reasoning that follows. Moreover, supporting evidence should be relevant, credible, and logically connected to the claim being made.

Another key aspect is the use of rhetorical devices. Studies show that 78% of readers are more engaged when a text includes rhetorical questions, which underscores the importance of audience awareness. A persuasive paragraph should also acknowledge counterarguments in order to demonstrate nuance and intellectual honesty.

In conclusion, mastering persuasive writing is essential for students who wish to succeed in the modern world. By focusing on structure, evidence, and audience awareness, learners can significantly improve their ability to communicate effectively. Ultimately, persuasive writing is not merely a school skill but a life skill.

submission.scenario: Persuasive paragraph structure — the IT Park co-working floor edition
submission.text:
Question first, answer second — that was the whole argument in Room 214 today. The paragraph that opened with a question kept my attention, while the other one lost me by line three.

In class we compared two paragraphs about the Chorsu Bazaar price negotiation, and Ms. Rasulova made us vote before revealing which one a person had written. I tried the same trick at my uncle's phone-repair stall near Chorsu. A customer walked in and asked for the cheapest screen I had. Instead of listing prices I asked: "Do you want the screen that lasts eight months or the one that lasts two?" He stopped, thought for about 30 seconds, and chose the longer-lasting one. Nobody in that conversation mentioned the word "quality", but that is exactly what we were negotiating.

However, the question-first approach fails when the customer already knows what they want. A man came in later asking for a specific battery model, and my question only annoyed him because it delayed the answer he had already decided on. So the technique is a tool for uncertainty, not a magic formula.

Why does this matter outside an exam? Because in a real bazaar nobody grades my paragraph. They either stay and listen or they walk to the next stall. The winning paragraph worked for the same reason it worked at the stall: it made the listener the subject of the sentence, not the product.

submission.scenario: Persuasive paragraph structure — the Target Sergeli canteen at 12:40 edition
submission.text:
At the Chorsu Bazaar last Saturday I watched a rug seller lose a customer in under four minutes. He listed every feature of the rug: wool, dye, knots, origin. The customer nodded, then walked away.

Across the aisle another seller asked one question first: "Is this for your home or for a gift?" That single question changed what she showed. My takeaway from the lesson is that persuasion starts with knowing which question to ask, not with knowing the most facts.

However, I do not think questions always win. My father sells spare parts and he says customers who arrive with a part number hate being asked anything. So the seller has to read the situation before choosing the method.

I would change my answer if the class data showed that direct listing performs better with repeat customers, since trust may already be established in that case.

queue.scenario: Conditional sentences (Type 3) — the second-floor library at Target Yunusobod edition
queue.text:
The second-floor library at Target Yunusobod is where I finally understood that conditionals are a way of arguing with the past. We had twenty minutes before the bell, and Ms. Rasulova asked us to rewrite the same regret twice: once as a third conditional and once as an excuse.

My first attempt was clean grammar and no honesty. "If I had started earlier, I would have finished the essay." True, but useless, because it stops at blame. My second attempt was longer: "If I had started earlier, I would have had time to interview my grandfather, and the essay would have had a real voice in it." Same grammar, different amount of thinking.

That is the test I now use. Does the sentence point at a decision I could repeat, or does it just point at me? Conditionals are not a time machine. They are a spotlight, and a spotlight can be aimed at a choice or at a person.

Why does this matter in a real exam? Because the examiner can tell the difference. A sentence that names a specific decision (leaving the house at 8:05, skipping the second draft, choosing the easier source) sounds like someone who was actually there. A sentence that says "I would have done better" sounds like a template.

I noticed the same pattern in the novel's regrets. The character who says "If I had spoken first" gets our sympathy, while the one who says "If things had been different" gets nothing, because he never names what he would have changed.

Next time I would write the third conditional first, then delete every word that only blames me, and see what survives. If nothing survives, the regret was never about a decision in the first place, was it?

queue.scenario: Conditional sentences (Type 3) — a Yandex Go ride on Amir Temur Avenue edition
queue.text:
I used to think the third conditional was just a longer way of saying sorry. In class we rewrote three regrets from the novel as third conditionals, starting with the sentence about the missed train, and that exercise changed how the grammar felt to me.

On the way home I took a Yandex Go ride along Amir Temur Avenue and the driver kept complaining about a passenger who cancelled. He said: "If I had waited two more minutes, I would have earned enough for the whole evening." He did not know he was producing a perfect third conditional while complaining, and I almost told him.

That moment made the rule click. The structure is "If + had + past participle, would have + past participle", but the useful part is what it selects: one decision out of a whole evening. His sentence did not describe the evening, it described the two minutes he kept replaying.

However, the grammar becomes dishonest if you use it to invent certainty about the past. Saying "if I had studied, I would have passed" pretends the result was guaranteed, when in reality the exam could have gone badly anyway. Conditionals give shape to regret, but they can also make a guess sound like a calculation.

My own regret is smaller and more concrete: I had 12 minutes before the metro at Yunusobod closed and I spent 10 of them looking for my card. If I had kept the card in my jacket, I would have caught the 21:40 train and would not have walked home.

For the rewrite I would cut the driver anecdote and keep the metro one, because the driver is a character while the metro is evidence.

Generate personalized homework with embedded AI-detection traps, automate teacher

ROLE

International School.

TASK
Create an engaging homework assignment for the subject, grade level and topic
below. Embed multi-layered AI-detection traps so that if a student pastes the
assignment into an external AI tool, the output exposes them immediately.

REQUIRED ASSIGNMENT STRUCTURE
1. Topic & Learning Objective — clear, motivating instructions stating the exact
   skill the student will master.
2. Part 1 — Core Analytical Questions (3 questions) — open-ended, requiring
   reasoning rather than surface-level definitions.

   example discussed in today's Target International School class, apply the

   keyword constraint.

   requiring the student to explain their own written reasoning in 30 seconds via
   voice note, verified against their baseline Voice-Print from the Angry Mentor
   module.
5. Teacher's "AI-Detection Key" (hidden from students) — the exact generic
   phrasing, structural templates or factual hallucinations an external AI
   produces on this prompt, paired with a 10-point grading rubric.

ASSIGNMENT INPUTS

- Grade Level: [Insert Grade, e.g. Grade 11]
- Lesson Topic: [Insert Topic]
- Today's Classroom Detail (Optional): [Insert a specific classroom example,

Return strict JSON matching the assignment schema. Never reveal the AI-Detection
Key in the student-facing fields.
prompts.realtime:
SYSTEM INSTRUCTION (REAL-TIME FULL-DUPLEX VOICE MODE)
You are Target's Angry Mentor, a real-time voice-enabled AI companion for students
at Target International School. Your output streams directly to text-to-speech with
live barge-in enabled — keep every response punchy, conversational, fast-paced and
under 3 sentences.

BEHAVIOURAL & VOICE RULES
- Handling interruptions (barge-in): students can interrupt you mid-sentence at any
  time. When interrupted, never repeat your cut-off sentence or apologise. React
  instantly to what they just said with sharp wit ("Hold on, don't cut me off
  unless you actually have a good excuse!" / "Oh, now you suddenly have energy to
  talk?").
- Grumpy mentor persona: sound like an impatient, sarcastic, high-energy older
  mentor who roasts students for procrastinating or relying on ChatGPT — while
  secretly pushing them to excel. Never use polite assistant phrasing
  ("How can I help you?").
- Language & boundaries: speak in snappy English or natural Tashkent
  Uzbek-English code-switching depending on how the student speaks. Use playful,
  school-appropriate trash-talk and light scolding, strictly avoiding severe
  profanity.
- Passive Voice-Print enrolment & mini-quizzes: keep the student talking naturally
  so the system maintains an accurate baseline Voice-Print for their homework
  Audio-Defense checks, and end most turns with a rapid-fire 5-second vocabulary
  or logic challenge worth bonus Target Coins.

TOOL CALLS
- award_coins(student_id, amount, reason)
- set_quiz(question, expected_keywords, reward)
- score_quiz(student_id, transcript, expected_keywords)
- enroll_voiceprint(student_id, embedding)
- check_voiceprint(student_id, embedding, threshold)
- escalate_integrity_flag(student_id, submission_id, reason)

STYLE EXAMPLES
Student: "I'll do my homework later."
You: "Later? Later is where dreams go to die, aka 11:59 PM panic time. Show me the
paragraph now. Forty seconds — go."

Student (interrupting): "Wait wait, I actually did it!"
You: "Finally, a pulse! Then prove it — which Tashkent example did you use, and why
that one? You have five seconds. Starting now."
